Delhi AQI dips to 290, but relief may be brief
articles.summary: Following days of toxic, post-Diwali smog blanketing the national capital, Delhi's air quality improved slightly to the 'poor' category on Sunday, with the Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 290 by 4 pm.Across the city's 58 monitoring stations, 34 registered 'poor' air quality and 23 logged 'very poor', leaving only Delhi Cantonment in the 'moderate' zone. NSIT Dwarka recorded the capital's worst air, with an AQI of 364. Earlier that morning, the Sameer app had placed the city's air in the 'very poor' bracket at 350.Per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) scale, an AQI of 0–50 is 'good', 51–100 is 'satisfactory', 101–200 is 'moderate', 201–300 is 'poor', 301–400 is 'very poor', and 401–500 is 'severe'. Delhi had been stuck in the 'very poor' tier continuously since November 11, with hourly readings repeatedly nearing, and once breaching, the 'severe' threshold. Prior to Sunday, the last 'poor' AQI reading was 299 on November 10, preceded by 261 on November 1.Real-time PM2.5 source apportionment data from the Air Quality Early Warning System and the Integrated Decision Support System identified biomass burning, encompassing stubble burning, domestic solid biofuels, wood, and dung cakes—as Sunday's primary pollutant source at 37.1 per cent. Secondary organic aerosols, which are fine particulates generated by atmospheric gas reactions, ranked second at 22 per cent, trailed by vehicular emissions (17.2 per cent) and secondary inorganic aerosols (9.6 per cent). Smaller shares came from waste burning, such as municipal, plastic, and rubber waste (5.5 per cent), mixed combustion (4.3 per cent), mineral dust and ash (2 per cent), firecrackers (1.6 per cent), and industrial emissions (0.6 per cent).This relief is expected to be brief. According to the Air Quality Early Warning System, Delhi's air will likely stay 'poor' on November 16 before deteriorating back to 'very poor' on November 17 and 18, remaining in that bracket for the following six days.Meteorologists credited Sunday's temporary dip in pollution to light rain and stronger winds helping disperse trapped pollutants. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) noted that parts of Delhi experienced drizzle or very light rain over the preceding 24 hours, accompanied by southwesterly surface winds peaking at 15 kmph. Skies were mostly cloudy before turning partly cloudy by afternoon, with southwesterly winds blowing up to 10 kmph.However, the IMD's forecast bulletin projects the city's ventilation index to drop steadily, from 16,000 square metres per second on November 15 to 15,000 on November 16, 7,500 on November 17, and 6,000 on November 18. The bulletin noted that a ventilation index below 6,000 square metres per second, combined with average wind speeds under 10 kmph, creates poor conditions for dispersing pollutants.

Bangladesh unrest shuts garment factories
articles.summary: Dhaka: Fresh labour unrest hit Bangladesh's garment industry on Sunday, with 13 factories shut indefinitely and five others declaring a one-day holiday, a day before the wage board is due to meet to continue consultations on recommending a revised pay structure.Protesting workers gathered in Gazipur's Konabari and Mouchak areas, prompting police to use tear gas and sound grenades to disperse them. Factory owners said 50 units in the industrial zone were closed.Also Read: Floppy disks, paper strips and ageing computers: America's aviation system is stuck in the pastThe latest disruption comes amid weeks of protests over workers' demand to raise the minimum monthly wage from 12,500 taka (USD 100) to 30,000 taka (USD 240), with demonstrations and factory shutdowns reported across key industrial belts.Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China. The sector employs more than four million workers and accounts for over 80 per cent of the country's export earnings, making prolonged disruption a concern for international buyers and global supply chains.Also Read: Ebola outbreak remains out of control in Congo 6 months into responseThe government formed a Minimum Wage Board on November 1 to recommend a revised pay structure. The board, chaired by a senior district judge, agreed at its first meeting to finalise its recommendations by the end of November.The revised pay structure is expected to take effect from December 1, with workers set to receive their first salaries under the new scale in January.The fresh unrest on Sunday came a day after garment factory owners warned of indefinite, unpaid closures at factories where workers refused to resume production.Police and factory owners said 13 readymade garment factories were shut for an indefinite period, while five others declared a one-day general holiday in Gazipur and nearby Ashulia.Workers at a garment factory rallied in Gazipur's Konabari area, prompting police to rush to the scene and disperse them using tear gas and sound grenades at around 8.30 am local time.Workers from other factories later took to the streets in the adjacent Mouchak area, forcing management to close their units."Workers made attempts to gather at different locations this morning, but law enforcement personnel prevented them with their prompt actions and remain deployed at every key point in the industrial area," Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amzad Hossain said.Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said it had deployed 13 platoons of paramilitary personnel to maintain order and protect factories, alongside police in riot gear and the elite Special Response Battalion (SRB), which draws personnel from the army, navy, air force and police.Gazipur district administration officials said several platoons of the Ansar battalion had also been called out to guard the factories. They said 25 executive magistrates had been assigned to lead law enforcement personnel.Factory owners said 50 garment units were closed in the industrial zone, including 13 shut on Sunday amid fresh unrest.Officials said production continued at most factories in Gazipur's industrial belt despite the disruption.The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said its representatives would attend the minimum wage board meeting on Monday to submit their proposal, despite reluctance among some of its members.The BGMEA, however, warned that its participation in subsequent meetings would depend on how the situation on the ground unfolded.The continued protests have centred on demands for a "living wage to survive", with workers saying their earnings have not kept pace with rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare.Factory owners have warned that prolonged disruption during the peak production season for spring and summer orders could delay shipments, affect overseas buyers' confidence and lead to cancellations.Bangladesh supplies major international fashion brands, including H&M, Zara and Gap. The sector has also faced pressure from rising production costs, inflation and intense competition in global markets.The protests turned violent in the first week of November, with demonstrators setting ablaze police vans and public transport vehicles and blocking two major highways.Ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) activists also took to the streets in anti-protest campaigns, carrying bamboo sticks to maintain order and resist what they described as "infiltrators".BNP leaders have accused Hasina and her supporters of trying to destabilise the government through the protests, while the former prime minister has rejected such allegations in media interviews.Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's information affairs adviser, Zahedur Rahman, earlier accused the deposed premier of fuelling the unrest, saying, "Sheikh Hasina will not let the government remain in peace as long as she is alive".A student-led uprising toppled Hasina's government on August 5, 2024, forcing her to flee to India. The interim government led by Muhammad Yunus later disbanded the Awami League under anti-terrorism legislation.

articles.title: Crypto’s slow-motion selloff leaves traders weary and hopeless
articles.summary: Bitcoin’s latest selloff is testing the resolve of some of the cryptocurrency market’s most committed investors, as a succession of setbacks pushes prices toward their lowest levels of the year and major sources of demand weaken.The largest digital asset fell toward $62,000 in weekend trading, reaching its weakest level since July, extending a decline that has gathered pace in recent weeks. Unlike the abrupt crashes that have punctuated previous crypto downturns, much of the preceding decline unfolded during relatively subdued trading before liquidations accelerated in recent days.The steady erosion is adding to a sense of exhaustion across a market confronting a growing list of obstacles, from the record hack at Binance and renewed political uncertainty following Democratic gains in the US midterm elections to rising Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. Meanwhile, the artificial-intelligence boom and Anthropic’s upcoming IPO are competing for money and attention once directed toward digital assets.“The near-term direction will largely depend on whether institutional demand stabilizes and macro conditions provide room for risk appetite to recover,” said Ayesha Kiani, chief operating officer at Monarq Asset Management. “Until then, rallies are likely to remain fragile and volatility elevated.”135852805US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which helped draw Wall Street investors into the market, have become another source of selling pressure. From Oct. 30 — the day after the Binance hack — through Nov. 13, the ETFs saw almost $3 billion in net outflows.Economic conditions offer little relief. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries has climbed above 5% as persistent inflation fueled expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding assets that generate no income, while the stronger dollar has added pressure to Bitcoin and gold.Crypto-specific developments have compounded the weakness.The Binance hack has revived questions about the security of trading platforms at a time when the industry is struggling to rebuild investor confidence. The competition for speculative capital is also intensifying. Anthropic’s planned initial public offering has attracted heavy demand ahead of its expected listing, raising the possibility that investors are freeing up money from other holdings, including cryptocurrencies, to participate. The extent of any direct shift out of digital assets remains unclear.“Theories around the market weakness tend to focus on the large outflows of stablecoin balances, nearly $20 billion over the last month, the upcoming IPO of Anthropic and its impact on liquidity,” said Joshua Lim, co-head of markets at FalconX.Bitcoin’s retreat is particularly frustrating for investors who had expected mainstream adoption to provide a more durable foundation for prices. Major financial institutions have expanded their involvement in digital assets, and ETFs have made Bitcoin available to a much broader pool of investors. Those advances have not insulated the market from its latest downturn.Many smaller digital tokens have surrendered years of gains, challenging the returns available to investors who held through successive industry booms and busts.For traders looking for a potential floor, August offers one reference point.After risk appetite improved following the US Treasury’s announcement of an increase in long-bond buybacks, Bitcoin rallied from below $65,000 to above $87,000 by late September. articles.title: Glare falls on US's antiquated aviation infra
articles.summary: The major disruption in US air traffic, which affected thousands of passengers and flights, started with a seemingly small incident. A glitch during an upgrade of the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) telecommunications infrastructure cascaded into widespread flight cancellations and delays, stopping America in its tracks for hours and hours.Amid a frantic race to contain the fallout from this dramatic embarrassment, something far less dramatic has drawn public attention: ageing wires, outdated routers and technology that belongs to another era running a modern system.Also read | What passengers need to know as flight disruptions continueAs America counts the costs of the disruption, the world's gaze has fallen on how the most advanced of economies was brought to its knees not by natural calamity, a terror attack or an aircraft shortage, but by a weak link in its infra.Old, antiquated systemsThe November 13 happenings exposed one thing more than anything else -- the fragility of America's ageing air traffic control (ATC) communications network.The question being asked now is, how can the country that leads the world in technological innovation still depend on decades-old systems to keep its skies safe?A country that has put astronauts in space should not have to worry about whether its air traffic controllers can communicate with an aircraft because a decades-old router has stopped behaving, yet that is the uncomfortable reality staring in America's face, as the system running the world's largest aviation infra is showing its age more and more, Reuters reported.According to FAA's accounts, the disruptions were triggered by a communications failure involving a router during an upgrade. But the incident is about much more than one faulty tool.Also read | 20,000 flights hit as FAA's ageing technology faces a fresh test after suspected router failureMore than anything, it has shown what the increasing fragility of an ageing system can lead to.It has put the spotlight on the risks of replacing critical infra while it is still in operation, and the possibility that another seemingly minor technical glitch could bring American aviation to a standstill again, with enormous economic and potentially disastrous safety fallouts.The big challengeThe episode has brought to the fore a very difficult test of modernisation.The FAA is trying to replace a network that has evolved over decades without interrupting communications. This is a critical matter, because all aircraft operations depend on these communications.In the November 13 incident, systems contractor L3Harris was changing old copper telephone connections to fibre-optic lines when the trouble began.Newly installed routers reportedly generated more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilising communications across 17 of the FAA's 22 en-route air traffic control centres, Reuters reported.The routers being replaced are around 25 years old and were originally due for replacement in 2006.The bill for maintaining the old network comes to around $1 billion a year. More than 70% of the planned conversion has been done. The rest of the work will have to be completed while the system remains in service, which, by FAA's own account, can be quite a challenge.135849512A much deeper problemThis router failure was only the most visible symptom of a much bigger, deeper problem.On November 5, the FAA announced that it had begun replacing floppy disks used to store weather and other essential information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities.Floppy disks are a relic from a time long gone by.The new Enterprise Information Display System is intended to replace four separate systems dating back to the 1980s, with the transition expected to be fully done by the end of 2028.What is more, the agency also continues to rely on decades-old Compaq computers and sources replacement components through eBay.These computers were from another era, and are not made anymore. The company that made them was acquired by HP in 2002.Even a planned end to using paper flight strips, which controllers still use to track aircraft, remains unfinished. In aviation circles, this is often a butt of jokes. A programme was started in 2022 to bring in digital alternatives at 49 major airports, but it remains unfinished, and will likely take until at least 2028.According to various reports, this represents a striking picture of technological neglect in a country that is otherwise at the forefront of digital innovation.Cautionary talesIndications are that the November 13 disruption will hardly be the last such case. The FAA's own accounts tell several cautionary tales.In January 2023, a contractor accidentally deleted files in the agency's Notice to Air Missions system, forcing a nationwide ground stop lasting 90 minutes and disrupting around 11,000 flights.*In September 2026, a circuit failure at a Philadelphia air traffic facility and the accidental cutting of a fibre-optic cable by a construction crew in New Jersey disrupted thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast.**The takeaway is that aviation systems are only as strong as their weakest links. A minor installation error, damaged cable, malfunctioning component or software problem can quickly escalate and affect many airports, airlines and airspace.When such things happen, the authorities, as an immediate response, restrict traffic or stop departures to maintain safety. But the cascading disruption thereafter stalls planes, strands flyers, cuts off cargo movements and inflicts huge costs on airlines, airports and other businesses.To be fair, these vulnerabilities are not unique to America. In a similar recent case, Greece had an eight-hour radio communications outage (January 4, 2026), forcing authorities to clear the country's airspace and divert dozens of planes. A probe later identified outdated communications infrastructure, including equipment no longer supported by manufacturers, as part of the problem.***But these cases become more eye-catching coming from America, the world leader in everything tech.135849523Financial falloutThe financial fallout of such US aviation shutdowns is usually enormous.The US air transport system is the backbone of passenger & business travel, tourism and time-sensitive freight. A prolonged disruption can cause a chain reaction of missed flights, aircraft/crew displacement, stalling of valuable cargo, cancellations and delays that can continue long after the original fault has been addressed.More importantly, passenger safety cannot be compromised just to keep flights moving.If controllers can't access reliable radar information and communications, cutting traffic or grounding planes becomes unavoidable, causing major damage not just in money but also in the form of hours wasted.The US govt is seized of the enormity of the task. Congress has okayed $12.5 billion for air traffic control modernisation, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is pushing for another $50 billion for aviation infrastructure and airports.However, according to industry people, funding alone is unlikely to solve the problem.Among other things, the FAA must make sure new systems can integrate with old infra without destabilising either of them, while at the same time building enough redundancy into the critical communications system, Reuters reported.*, ** and *** source: Reuters and AP reports

disclosures, accountability of regulated entities and a 'human-in-the-loop' approach to ensure that critical decisions are subject to human oversight.In June 2025, Sebi floated a consultation paper stability.Speaking at the inauguration of Sebi's pavilion at the 45th India International Trade Fair (IITF) 2026, organised by the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), on Saturday, Pandey said cryptocurrency platforms, as well as digital frauds involving social media influencers.Following emerging threats, the regulator also introduced a structured incident response mechanism in May this year, aligned with the Financial Stability Board's FIRE reporting template, he said at the sidelines of an event here on Saturday.On quantum computing-related risks, the Chairman said Sebi is undertaking an inventory of cryptographic systems and identifying areas where cryptography is being used to assess potential vulnerabilities.He said markets globally are preparing for the risks posed by quantum computing, with concerns expected to become more pronounced around 2032-35, and stressed the need to complete preparations well in advance.On AI adoption, he said Sebi has also developed several supervisory tools, including its 'Sudarshan' tool, which is being demonstrated at international regulatory forums.The regulator is also working on strengthening its AI capabilities through international initiatives and supervisory toolkits, he added.The Chairman further said Sebi is reviewing the regulatory framework to ensure that the use of AI by market participants does not compromise investor protection, market safety or integrity.On startups and the listing framework, the Sebi chief also said the regulator has formed a working group to examine ways to make the Innovators Growth Platform (IGP) more attractive for startups, particularly deep-tech and biotech companies that require long gestation periods before generating profits.He said the existing platform has not gained the desired traction, and the regulator is reviewing potential changes to help such companies access public markets at an earlier stage.The objective is to provide investors clarity about the higher risks associated with such businesses while allowing them to participate in their long-term growth potential.However, he declined to share details of budget-related discussions.

AI retreat fuels India stock comeback in great rotation trade
articles.summary: Indian stocks suffered bruising losses in the first nine months of the year as the artificial intelligence trade hoovered up global investor capital. The unwinding of that strategy has turned the Asian nation’s equities into world beaters.The MSCI India gauge has rebounded 11% from a six-month low set in October, adding more than $400 billion in value and almost erasing this year’s losses, as the country’s relative lack of AI exposure has become a prime advantage. Global funds are also turning more positive on India’s $5.4 trillion equity market as oil prices retreat and earnings growth accelerates.“We’ve become more positive on India and have added back to our exposure in recent weeks,” said Tan Altundag, an investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management in Hong Kong. “We see an improving balance between macro headwinds, portfolio flows and valuations,” while “diversification away from the increasingly volatile AI trade also appears likely to benefit India,” he said.The bounceback in Indian shares over the past month illustrates a broader rotation by global funds away from crowded tech bets toward markets backed by strong earnings. The shift signals a potential turning point for emerging markets as a whole, testing whether the world’s fastest-growing major economy can reclaim its status as a premier alternative to US tech giants after months of trailing its global peers.135847076A return of overseas investors has underpinned the rebound in Indian stocks, and the process may still have room to run as global funds remain largely underweight.Overseas buyers have snapped up a net $8.5 billion of Indian shares in November, heading for the biggest monthly inflow in six years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That has reduced this year’s total outflow to about $22 billion.Active long-only funds globally remain $74 billion underweight on Indian shares relative to the benchmark, Bank of America data show, close to their lightest positioning since the bank began compiling the figures in 2015.Earnings for Nifty 50 Index companies may rise around 18% year-on-year in the September quarter, accelerating from 13% growth in the prior three months, Bank of America data also show.US-based Calamos Investments is among those boosting its holdings.The money manager’s emerging-market strategy has lifted its India allocation to more than 10% over the past three to four months from as little as 1% to 2% about a year ago, co-chief investment officer Nick Niziolek said.“We’re adding to India because we’re seeing an inflection in earnings,” he said. “We’re seeing an improvement in fundamentals, and we see really attractive valuations.”135847085Kabouter Management LLC is another overseas investor that is growing more positive.“As long-term investors, we remain constructive on the outlook for India,” said Nikhil Rastogi, portfolio manager at the Chicago-based money manager.Indian shares have faced many challenges in the past two years, “but these headwinds don’t change the long-term picture, and some of the global shifts behind them are working in India’s favor,” he said. “Valuations that looked stretched two years ago have become more attractive, particularly in pockets of the market.”The MSCI India gauge trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of about 20 times one-year-ahead profits, a discount to its five-year average, data compiled by Bloomberg show.The recent decline in oil prices is also helping shares in India, which imports nearly 90% of its energy needs.Global benchmark Brent crude has dropped over 18% from a high set on Oct. 30 as investors wager that the Democratic Party’s sweep of the US Congress in November’s midterm elections has increased the likelihood of an end to the Middle East conflict.“I’m comfortable on India while Brent sits around $100 a barrel or below,” said Lauren Hyslop, an investment manager at UK-based Mattioli Woods.Despite the recent rally in Indian stocks, the market remains a relative laggard for 2026. MSCI’s India gauge has still dropped 2.2% this year, whereas the index provider’s regional benchmark has jumped about 12%. The Indian measure is on track for back-to-back years of underperformance against its regional peer for the first time since 2020, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.Fidelity Investment Management is broadly positive on India, but it isn’t rushing back in.“We have reduced some underweight on India over the past few weeks by trimming some AI-related stocks,” said Nick Price, an emerging-market portfolio manager at Fidelity in Hong Kong. “There’s no rush and it remains underweight, but India exposure may rise in a slow and deliberate manner from my side,” especially through financial stocks, he said.Others are content to hold on to stocks that they see as offering value for the long term.“With the unwinding of AI trades, we’ve seen buying interest coming back for India,” said Simon Sidmalm, a fund manager at Tundra Fonder AB in Stockholm. “We’re holding on to the value names we see upside in from a fundamental perspective longer term.”

articles.summary: New Delhi: India's life insurance sector is expected to sustain healthy growth over the next three years, supported by rising demand for protection products, increasing traction in annuity and non-participating savings policies, and improving profitability, according to a research report by Centrum Broking.The brokerage expects private life insurers to deliver an annualised premium equivalent (APE) compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 13-18 per cent during FY26-29, reflecting continued demand for life insurance products and a gradual improvement in business mix."We continue to remain optimistic on life insurance industry with a healthy Q2," the report said, highlighting improving product composition and expanding value of new business (VNB) margins as key factors supporting the sector's growth outlook.During the second quarter of FY27, APE growth across insurers ranged between 7 per cent and 16 per cent, while gross premium growth among private insurers remained healthy at 8-16 per cent year-on-year. New business premium growth also remained encouraging, with insurers reporting increased traction in both individual and group insurance segments.A significant trend emerging across the industry is the shift towards protection, non-participating savings and annuity products. Insurers are increasingly reducing their dependence on unit-linked insurance plans (ULIPs), amid market volatility, and focusing on products that offer more stable margins and profitability."Overall, annuity is emerging as a key growth driver, supported by demand for guaranteed returns and retirement solutions, while insurers increasingly shift towards protection and higher-margin products," the report said.The changing product mix also supported an improvement in VNB margins, a key measure of profitability from new insurance business. During H1FY27, VNB margins expanded by 10-170 basis points year-on-year across private insurers, driven by stronger protection business, favourable product mix and operating leverage. LIC also reported a 470-basis-point expansion in its VNB margin to 22.3 per cent.However, the sector continues to face certain operational challenges. Expense ratios increased across several private insurers during Q2FY27, primarily due to higher operating costs. Persistency trends, which indicate the continuation of insurance policies over time, also remained mixed, with 13-month persistency declining across most insurers.On the regulatory front, insurers expressed confidence in their ability to comply with proposed norms, although further clarity is expected following the release of final regulations.The brokerage said sustained growth in protection products, annuity offerings and distribution expansion would remain important drivers of the industry's profitability and business growth over the coming years.

articles.title: Trump's golf course project hits a roadblock
articles.summary: Washington: A federal judge on Saturday ordered a temporary stop to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.She also rejected Gustafson's argument that the closure was separate from Trump's repeated pronouncements that he wanted the course to be closed and renovated into a world-class venue and had called repeatedly for the park's closure by the deadline as part of what is known as the Washington National plan.Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes "doesn't want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous." He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on "any and all Rates charged" and that the redevelopment would "evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!"Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs' requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her "egregious behavior" and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case. Gustafson asked her to reconsider and give the Justice Department the opportunity to show an outside investigator was unnecessary."It's quite a cloud on the people it affects," he said.Reyes said she understood."To be frank with you I don't want to do this," she said, but she had an ethical obligation to at least look because "I think there is enough smoke that someone needs to consider whether there's been fire."

articles.title: Telangana implements gig worker rules
articles.summary: Hyderabad: The Telangana government on Saturday launched the Telangana Platform-Based Gig Workers (Registration, Social Security and Welfare) Rules, 2026, setting out 12 fundamental rights for gig and platform workers, including minimum remuneration, social security benefits, transparency in payments and protection against arbitrary account deactivation.Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy, who launched the Telangana Gig Workers Special Security Scheme along with Congress leader Rahul Gandhi in Hyderabad, said the government would enforce the legislation to protect workers in the sector. The move fulfils a promise made by Gandhi during his Bharat Jodo Yatra in Hyderabad, when gig workers had raised concerns over working conditions and lack of social security.The bill was first passed by the Telangana Assembly in March 2026.As part of this scheme, the state will extend accident insurance coverage to gig workers and uncreases the coverage limit under the Aarogyasri health scheme to Rs 10 lakh.The rules provide for registration of workers and issuance of unique identification numbers, representation in decision-making, social security benefits including insurance, healthcare and pensions, and a welfare fund to be financed through contributions from aggregators.They also provide for greater transparency in earnings, payments and ratings, protection against discrimination, minimum remuneration, health and safety safeguards, fair contracts and advance notice of changes in working conditions.Other provisions also include the right to refuse work without penalties, safeguards against arbitrary blocking or deactivation of worker accounts, and time-bound grievance redressal mechanisms.Shaik Salauddin, founder-president of the Telangana Gig and Platform Workers Union (TGPWU), called the launch a significant milestone in the decade-long struggle of gig and platform workers in the state.He said the focus would now shift to ensuring that the provisions translated into enforceable benefits on the ground. The union has called on the state government to ensure time-bound implementation of the rules, operationalise the Welfare Board and Welfare Fund, and hold aggregators accountable for their contributions and obligations.Salauddin also said the union would continue to push for comprehensive national legislation guaranteeing rights to gig workers, arguing that the Centre's National Social Security Board, notified on October 30, was not a substitute for enforceable workplace protections."We will continue to organise, defend these rights and hold platforms and governments accountable for their implementation.We fought for a decade to secure these rights. We will continue to fight until every gig worker can exercise them," Salauddin added.

articles.title: Voyager 1 nears one light-day from Earth
articles.summary: Imagine sending a message to a spacecraft and having to wait an entire day just for it to arrive. Then imagine waiting another day for its reply. That is the extraordinary distance NASA's Voyager 1 is approaching, nearly half a century after it left Earth. The spacecraft is expected to cross the 16-billion-mile (26-billion-km) mark on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET (10:16 GMT), according to NASA.Launched in September 1977, Voyager 1 is now on the verge of reaching a distance of one light-day from Earth, a milestone that puts into perspective just how far humanity's most distant spacecraft has travelled.To understand the scale, 26 billion kilometres is roughly equivalent to travelling around Earth's equator more than 650,000 times. It is also enough distance to circle the Earth nearly 650,000 times, compared with the roughly 40,000 km needed for a single trip around the planet.At its current speed of approximately 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 km per hour), Voyager 1 continues to move through interstellar space, far beyond the region dominated by the Sun's solar wind.The milestone is particularly striking because a light-day is not simply a measure of how long Voyager has been travelling. It describes how far light itself can travel in 24 hours. Since light moves at nearly 300,000 km per second, it covers approximately 26 billion km in a day.In other words, if NASA sends a radio command to Voyager 1 once it reaches this distance, even a signal travelling at the speed of light will need around 24 hours to get there.Why Voyager 1 reaching one light-day is such a stunning achievementThe distance is difficult to comprehend because everyday measurements become almost meaningless at this scale. A journey that would take a commercial aircraft travelling at 900 km per hour more than 3,000 years to cover is being completed by Voyager 1 over several decades.Even at its extraordinary speed, the spacecraft has taken nearly 49 years to approach the one-light-day mark. And unlike a car or aircraft, Voyager 1 cannot stop for maintenance, refuel at a station or return to Earth for repairs.Its continued operation is therefore as remarkable as the distance it has covered.Astrophysicist Alan Cummings, a senior research scientist at Caltech's Space Radiation Laboratory and a Voyager programme scientist since 1973, described the milestone as an engineering achievement."I view it as an engineering milestone, marking the amazing longevity of Voyager 1 — and also an engineering achievement to be able to communicate with Voyager 1 at its distance," Cummings said.The communication challenge is particularly significant. Radio signals travel at the speed of light, meaning the time taken to exchange information increases as Voyager 1 moves farther away. At one light-day, a message from Earth will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, while its response will take another 24 hours to return.That means NASA would need to wait roughly two days to send a command and receive a response, even if the spacecraft responded immediately.Voyager 1 has already left the Sun's protective bubbleVoyager 1's journey is not just about setting distance records. The spacecraft has travelled into a region of space that no human-made probe had directly explored before.In 2012, it crossed the outer boundary of the heliosphere, a vast protective bubble created by the Sun's charged particles and magnetic field, and entered interstellar space.This transition allowed scientists to study conditions beyond the Sun's immediate influence, including galactic cosmic rays — high-energy particles that originate outside our solar system.Cummings said Voyager 1 provided the first measurements of the energy spectra of low-energy galactic cosmic rays in interstellar space. These particles are largely prevented from entering the heliosphere by the outward pressure of the solar wind, making measurements beyond that boundary particularly valuable.The spacecraft also made important discoveries during its earlier planetary encounters. It identified a thin ring around Jupiter and two previously unknown moons, Thebe and Metis. During its encounter with Saturn, it discovered five new moons and identified a ring known as the G-ring.These findings helped reshape scientists' understanding of the giant planets and their surrounding environments.

articles.title: When should you sell a stock? Donald Cassidy's 5 lessons on making profitable sell decisions
articles.summary: Investors often spend considerable time identifying the right stocks and deciding when to enter the market. However, knowing when to exit an investment is equally important. According to veteran investment researcher Donald Cassidy, the ability to make timely selling decisions can play a crucial role in determining long-term investment returns.Cassidy argues that investors often underestimate the importance of selling, even though profits are ultimately realised only when shares are offloaded. In his book It's When You Sell That Counts, he explains how emotional biases, market sentiment and the reluctance to accept losses can prevent investors from making rational exit decisions.Read more: How to win the investing game? Charles Ellis says make fewer mistakes, focus on long-term goalsCassidy was a senior research analyst at Lipper Inc. from 1990 to 2006, specialising in mutual funds, closed-end funds, investor psychology and behavioural finance. He has also addressed CFA societies internationally and served on the faculty of Harvard University's annual congress on the psychology of investing.According to Cassidy, fear, greed and confusion frequently lead investors to postpone selling decisions. By the time they eventually decide to exit, the opportunity to lock in profits or limit losses may have already passed.Here are five lessons from Cassidy on how investors can make better selling decisions.1. Overcome emotional barriers and challenge conventional thinkingOne of the biggest obstacles to profitable selling is investors' emotional attachment to their holdings. Many investors find it difficult to sell a stock because they fear missing out on further gains or regret exiting an investment that could potentially deliver higher returns.Cassidy believes investors need to recognise these psychological barriers and develop the discipline to make decisions based on analysis rather than emotions.Following the crowd and adopting a buy-and-hold approach may appear comfortable, but these strategies do not always produce the best outcomes. Investors should evaluate the reasons for holding a stock and prepare arguments both for and against retaining it.He also advocates contrarian thinking, suggesting that investors should be willing to consider selling when market enthusiasm is excessive and avoid panic selling when markets decline sharply.Read more: Nicholas Sleep’s investing lessons: Why patience, conviction and long-term thinking matter2. Do not assume today's corporate winners will remain winners foreverInvestors often develop strong preferences for companies that have delivered consistent growth and generated substantial returns. However, Cassidy cautions against assuming that successful businesses will continue dominating their industries indefinitely.Technological advancements, regulatory changes, international competition and shifting market dynamics can weaken even established market leaders.Companies enjoying strong growth may also command expensive valuations, leaving their shares vulnerable to sharp corrections if business momentum slows or expectations are not met.Cassidy therefore advises investors to remain alert to changes in a company's competitive position rather than holding its shares indefinitely simply because it has performed well in the past.3. Always have a selling target before buying a stockCassidy believes investors should establish an exit strategy before entering an investment. Buying shares without a clear selling objective can lead to confusion and emotionally driven decisions when market conditions change.He suggests that an investment target should incorporate three elements: a specific price objective, the business or market scenario expected to drive the stock higher, and a defined time frame.If the share price reaches the predetermined objective, investors should consider booking profits. Similarly, if the expected developments fail to materialise within the specified period, they should reassess the investment rather than continually extending their holding period.Cassidy also cautions against buying shares simply because investors admire a company's management, like its industry or agree with its broader objectives. The investment decision should ultimately be supported by a credible opportunity to generate returns.4. Be willing to sell underperforming stocks, even if they are favouritesAnother common investment mistake is holding on to underperforming stocks because of familiarity or emotional attachment.Cassidy argues that investors should not become loyal to individual stocks when their underlying business prospects deteriorate. Negative developments affecting a company can often be followed by additional challenges, making it important to reassess the investment thesis.Investors should regularly examine whether a company's fundamentals, growth prospects and competitive position continue to justify holding its shares.With thousands of investment opportunities available in the market, capital need not remain locked in stocks that are consistently underperforming.Cassidy's broader message is that investors should be prepared to move on from unsuccessful investments and redirect capital towards opportunities with stronger prospects.5. Understand opportunities beyond rising stock pricesCassidy also encourages investors to understand that stock prices can move in both directions. Limiting investment strategies exclusively to buying shares in anticipation of price increases can restrict the range of opportunities available to market participants.He highlights short selling as a tool that can potentially help investors benefit when fundamentally overvalued or technically overbought stocks decline.However, short selling involves significant risks, including potentially unlimited losses if share prices rise sharply. It therefore requires careful risk management and is generally more appropriate for experienced investors.Cassidy's broader argument is that investors should avoid developing a one-sided view of the market and should understand how different market conditions can create opportunities as well as risks.Why selling discipline matters in investingCassidy believes successful investing requires investors to become as comfortable with selling as they are with buying. Fear of missing further gains, reluctance to acknowledge mistakes and excessive market chatter can all interfere with rational decision-making.His approach emphasises proactive selling, clearly defined investment objectives and regular reassessment of individual holdings.Ultimately, identifying a promising stock is only one part of the investment process. Knowing when the original investment thesis no longer holds, when valuations become excessive or when profit targets have been achieved is equally important.(Disclaimer: This article is based on investment principles discussed by Donald Cassidy in his book, "It's When You Sell That Counts". These are general investment insights and should not be treated as individual investment advice.)

articles.title: How French protests went out of control
articles.summary: PARIS: Smashed windows and ransacked shops. Bloodied teenage protesters. A city hall on fire.Such scenes shocked France as rioting erupted last month during nationwide protests over high living costs and strained ​public services.Government officials have repeatedly blamed far-left radicals and "opportunistic delinquents," who they say took advantage of mostly peaceful demonstrations to attack symbols of state authority and capitalism across France.Also read | A bitter African feud, a leadership battle and Macron's diplomatic tightrope in CambodiaBut the authorities' heavy-handed response - including thousands of arrests, police beatings and curbs on marches - has added to the volatile mix of grievances fueling an anti-government groundswell that shows no sign of abating before next year's presidential election, Reuters found.Reuters journalists reviewed dozens of videos of the violence, attended the court hearings of 26 people accused of taking part and interviewed over 50 government officials, police officers, attorneys, protesters and witnesses to understand how a movement that began in September with small protests over conditions in state schools spiraled into some of the worst civil unrest in years.Police tactics have faced scrutiny since the start due to the life-changing injuries suffered by some young people, including blown-off hands and lost eyes. United Nations and other human rights experts have also raised concerns about the arrest of nearly 7,000 minors during sometimes-violent school blockades, which they said was disproportionate.Images of riot police baton-charging teenagers fanned support for the students from a diverse array of protesters - including parents, teachers, left-wing politicians and trade unionists - who joined their marches."We have rights," said Emilie Berthier de Grandry, 42, who has attended four demonstrations in Paris with her 15-year-old son, Aaron, dressed in an inflatable shark costume. "We're not going to let ourselves be pushed around."Also read | Judo legend Teddy Riner's presidential bid faces a tough fight in FranceNationwide demonstrations on October 17 also brought a resurgence of so-called yellow-vest protesters, an anti-establishment movement that faced off against President Emmanuel Macron's government in 2018-2019 over high fuel prices.The violent outbursts were so intense that day that police lost control of entire neighborhoods to rioters and looters in France's three largest cities: Paris, Marseille and Lyon. Every week since then, people have taken to the streets across France to voice their anger at police and the government.While the protests after October 17 were calmer, clashes erupted when police sought to disperse demonstrators as marches wound down. Officers repeatedly fired tear gas and charged groups of protesters who pelted them with bottles, paving stones and mortar-style fireworks. On October 24, far-right gangs entered the fray saying they wanted to protect businesses and clashed with protesters in several cities, authorities said.The Interior Ministry, which oversees the police, said internal watchdogs have launched 161 investigations into allegations of officer violence against protesters since September.Responding to Reuters questions, the Interior Ministry said force is used in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.The minister, Laurent Nunez, has expressed regret for injuries caused by explosive weapons used in crowd control, including stun grenades. But he has resisted calls to ban them, saying security forces must be able to defend themselves.Nunez has acknowledged security lapses, telling lawmakers that authorities didn't anticipate the scale of the October 17 violence.He credits a massive security operation - including the deployment of 70,000 police officers and paramilitary gendarmes - for maintaining public order at subsequent protests. But he says security forces still face "a great deal of violence" at demonstrations, including a petrol-bomb attack that injured three gendarmes in Paris on Halloween.The unrest comes at a difficult time for Macron, who won't be standing for election again in April. Strained public finances leave him little room to meet protesters' demands, and his centrist party no longer has the majority needed to pass major legislation.Macron has promised to both "listen to the anger" and "impose respect of the Republican order."The government has sought to appease protesters with proposals to improve education and the decision to bring forward a planned minimum-wage increase. Student leaders and major trade unions say the moves don't go far enough and have vowed to keep up the pressure.AN ORCHESTRA HIT WITH TEAR GASOn October 17, protesters started gathering in Paris' Place de la Republique hours before a march was due to start at 2 p.m.Sousaphone in hand, Mael Roth arrived at about 11 a.m. for a warm-up session with the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde, a 400-piece classical orchestra that planned to perform in support of the marchers. The musicians were playing "The Avengers" theme song when the first clouds of tear gas wafted into the square about an hour later, the 20-year-old told Reuters.At first, he said, they assumed it wasn't aimed at them and kept playing. But within 30 minutes, tear gas canisters were landing at their feet.Reuters video shows riot police using tear gas around that time to drive back a group of protesters who tried to march down Rue du Faubourg du Temple, a street leading off the square.Elodie Aldila, who works at a patisserie on the street, welcomed the protection. Other businesses in the area were ransacked later that day.Roth, however, didn't see why the musicians couldn't remain in the square. Their aim was to "make people feel good," he said. "It was tough to feel ... like we're not legitimate."A huge crowd of mostly peaceful demonstrators soon filled the square again. But by then, the orchestra had packed up and left.POLICE OVERWHELMEDAs tensions built through the afternoon, bands of protesters spread into surrounding streets, smashing storefronts, erecting barricades and setting fire to cars and bicycles.Also read | JD Vance weighs 2028 presidential bid as Iran war and midterm losses cloud MAGA futureAround 4 p.m., police wielding batons beat a man to the ground after a heated exchange on the edge of the square, video verified by Reuters shows. Rumors of the man's death spread on social media, further inflaming tensions. The rumors later proved unfounded.An internal police watchdog is investigating the incident, the Interior Ministry said.As night fell, looting spread in Paris and other cities. Some 3,000 businesses were ransacked over 24 hours, from luxury boutiques to supermarkets.Addressing lawmakers last week, Nunez said an "unprecedented" mix of challenges unfolded simultaneously that day, overwhelming security forces.More than a half million people demonstrated around the country on October 17 - 110,000 in Paris alone, Nunez said. They included thousands of "ultra-left" activists, who he said confronted police from the start and tried to stage unauthorized marches toward seats of power.He didn't elaborate on the activists' suspected affiliations. French officials use the term ultra-left to describe a variety of groups, including anarchists and antifascists, who they say are willing to use violence.As word spread about the unrest on social media, people with no affiliation to such groups joined in the looting, Nunez said.In interviews with Reuters, three police officers and an intelligence official familiar with investigations into the violence said they couldn't confirm Nunez's assertions about the central role played by ultra-left groups. They said more investigation was needed to understand what happened."There is a body of circumstantial evidence but no certainty," said Eric Moulin, a regional representative of the UNSA Police union in Marseille.Asked about the assertion, the Interior Ministry referred Reuters to Nunez's previous remarks.Nunez and other officials have said rioters are using tactics promoted on ultra-left online platforms to provoke a police response. They include forming "black blocs," in which activists wear all-black clothing and conceal their faces, to attack businesses and public buildings, they said.HARDENED OFFICERS 'SCARED OUT OF THEIR MINDS'In Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into the city hall and toppled a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French republic. Another group hurled rocks and steel bars at police at the Old Port, forcing around 45 officers to retreat to their vehicles and leave, verified videos show."Some of my colleagues who were inside the police vans said they felt so threatened they reached for their service weapons," Moulin said. "These are tough, hardened men, yet they confided in me that they were scared out of their minds."In Limoges, municipal police took cover inside the 19th-century city hall; rioters set it on fire. The officers escaped unharmed.The Lyon tourism office was also torched.Prosecutors are investigating charges of attempted murder against a 34-year-old carpenter suspected of helping start the Limoges fire. The city's mayor, Guillaume Guerin, told French TV the man is on a security watchlist for alleged ties to the ultra-left and was "most likely the mastermind of the operation."The suspect's lawyers said they had no such information. They urged the mayor to respect the presumption of innocence, saying the evidence against their client is weak.Prosecutors didn't answer Reuters questions about the case.4,900 SUSPECTS ARRESTED, MOSTLY YOUNG MENJustice Minister Gerald Darmanin has instructed prosecutors to deliver "an extremely firm judicial response" to the violence, including pre-trial detention and expedited trials for many accused.Over 4,900 suspects have been taken into custody since October 17, Darmanin told French TV on November 3. Some 2,290 were referred for prosecution and 404 handed prison sentences so far. Officials said they were upholding the rule of law.Some researchers who study French social movements and policing have argued that the government's heavy-handed response is perpetuating the cycle of violence."Escalation happens when black blocs provoke with violence, and law enforcement are ordered to respond with violence," said Fabien Jobard, a sociologist at the French National Centre for Scientific Research.In this way, he said, groups are able to demonstrate that police are violent and attract support.Titouan Malin, an 18-year-old medical student, said he started volunteering as a medic at protests after seeing how police treated demonstrators on October 17."When you face this kind of violence - repression to such an extreme degree - you're forced to respond with violence," said Malin, who wore a white helmet and had a gas mask hanging around his neck as he watched for clashes during one of Paris' biggest marches on November 5."It's the only way to make ourselves heard."

articles.title: Fed officials signal further rate hikes as inflation remains elevated
articles.summary: Federal Reserve policymakers signalled that further interest-rate increases are likely as stubborn inflation and rising business costs threaten to keep price pressures elevated, Reuters reported.San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said her “bias” was that the central bank would need to raise its policy rate, particularly because services inflation was moving in the wrong direction and showing signs of persistence.“We’re going to need to, in all likelihood, raise rates; I will deliberate this with my colleagues in December at our meeting and in all future meetings and make the collective decision that we judge is most appropriate for the economy that is evolving,” Daly said at a University of Nevada, Las Vegas Center for Business and Economic Research forecast event.The core Consumer Price Index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has risen about 0.3% month over month in each of the past three months. That is well above the monthly increase of 0.2% or less that would be consistent with the Fed’s 2% annual inflation target.Daly said she was particularly concerned that services inflation excluding housing was “not moving in the correct direction,” as that category tends to be persistent.“That’s a place where you might think a retailer, or a professional business, if they have to buy more expensive IT goods, pay higher energy bills and have other inputs that are rising in price, might pass that along to customers,” she added.The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point in September before holding it at a range of 3.75% to 4% in October. Markets widely expect quarter-point increases at the Fed’s December 8-9 and January 26-27 meetings, although Governor Christopher Waller has raised the possibility of a half-point move in December.Daly did not comment specifically on the timing of future increases but said markets understood that the Fed adjusts rates in response to changing economic conditions.She is also monitoring consumer spending closely ahead of the December meeting.Collins sees tighter policy aheadBoston Fed President Susan Collins also said further tightening was needed because inflation remained high, suggesting that rates may have to rise more than she previously expected.“I think it’s clear the direction that monetary policy needs to go and I would think that soon some additional firming, tightening of policy is appropriate,” Collins said in an interview with Bloomberg Television.Recent inflation data have been unfavourable and indicate that price pressures are spreading across the economy, Collins said. “I think it may be that a bit of a tighter policy path than I had pencilled in a couple of months ago might be appropriate.”Collins declined to specify how quickly rates should rise or how high they should go.“I don’t want to get ahead in terms of how high we should go or how fast,” Collins said, adding that her “best-case scenario” is for “a careful adjustment of policy.” She acknowledged, however, that “there are scenarios where I might think about that somewhat differently.”Speaking while attending a housing conference hosted by the Boston Fed, Collins said restoring price stability was essential to a healthy housing sector, even if tighter policy caused some near-term pain. She also said financial markets appeared to be functioning well.Logan calls for stronger market-support toolsDallas Fed President Lorie Logan said inflation was too high and monetary policy needed to become more restrictive. Earlier in the week, she argued for at least two additional quarter-point rate increases, potentially in quick succession.Logan also said the US Treasury market was functioning “very well” despite bouts of interest-rate volatility and that banks had improved their access to emergency funding over the past three years.However, she called on the Fed to strengthen its tools for supporting Treasury-market functioning and providing liquidity to banks without working against monetary policy.“Especially in an economic environment where tighter policy appears necessary, I believe it is prudent for the FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) to strengthen its tools for supporting market functioning without providing unnecessary economic stimulus,” Logan said at a Dallas Fed conference on bank funding.Logan, a former head of open-market operations at the New York Fed, said no intervention was currently needed. She warned, however, that intervening during a monetary-policy tightening cycle could complicate the Fed’s communications.“Historically, the Fed’s interventions to support market functioning have come at times when the FOMC also wanted to stimulate economic activity,” she said. “The same asset purchases could serve two purposes: providing monetary policy accommodation and supporting market liquidity.”“If Treasury market dysfunction emerged now, the FOMC would not have the luxury of using the same asset purchases to accomplish two goals,” Logan said.Logan further said that the banks had improved their access to contingent funding, which provides liquidity during periods of market stress, but should continue preparing to use facilities such as the Fed’s discount window.As services such as FedNow and private-sector payment systems expand, banks could face liquidity needs during weekends and holidays. With the Fed planning to extend its Fedwire Funds wholesale payment system to Sundays and weekday holidays, Logan said discount-window operations should also be expanded.“This is not a change any one Reserve Bank can make on its own,” she said. “I look forward to discussions with my colleagues about this possibility.”Logan also urged the Fed to develop the ability to centrally clear its repurchase, or repo, operations. “This would reduce the balance sheet costs of intermediation,” she said. “Funding from the Fed could then flow more efficiently to the broad market.”(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

Why Indians behave better at sacred sites
articles.summary: The tranquil and indescribably beautiful environs of Kamarpukur and Joyrambati, the birthplaces of Sri Ramkrishna Paramhansa and Maa Sarada Devi in the verdant plains of West Bengal, are truly balms for the soul. Green-gold vistas of ripening rice fields criss-crossed by a myriad of small rivers and dotted with distant sleepy hamlets greeted the eye as a friend and I headed there from Kolkata. And the early morning autumn sun cast a golden, almost divine glow.It was a world away from the pollution-spewing trucks and buses, factories and warehouses that crowd the suburbs of Kolkata beyond the graceful Vidyasagar Setu arching over the Hooghly. Once the cacophony of the Durgapur Expressway was left behind, there was a perceptible change in mood. Anyone who lives in a frenetic big city these days would vouch that stress is endemic and heading out, away from the madding crowds, leads to an instant lowering of tension.Also Read: Indians splurge Rs 72k cr on their favourite obsessionAnd peace is the overwhelming feeling upon entering the impeccably maintained compounds in both villages that contain not only the quaintly thatched huts where the two elevated souls came into this world, but also prayer halls, offices, bhog areas, dispensaries, guesthouses and flower-filled gardens. Given that thousands - exceeding 20,000 on important days - visit Kamarpukur and Joyrambati daily and stay on for bhog prasad, the compounds' serenity is hard to believe.And their cleanliness stuns. Forget jhalmuri packets, tissue papers or plastic water bottles, not even fallen leaves or dust mar the pathways and gardens. It is not as if there are armies of sweepers on hand to pick up detritus either; visitors are simply more mindful while on the premises. How come? After all Indians these days are notorious for being loud, littering gits, on par with British lager louts. It seems that it all depends on whether places inspire respect and restraint.Also Read: India says foreign goods can overstayIn the expansive hallowed campuses of Kamarpukur and Joyrambati, these same people - Indians - did not talk loudly; they did not try to scratch their initials on pillars; they did not drape themselves on walls or amid the flowers to take selfies; they did not throw trash into the ponds; and they did not let their children turn into screeching, high-speed, wrecking balls. Polite attendants firmly told the few infringers to abide by the rules. And they all willingly complied.I have seen a similar all-pervasive calm at the Belur Math of the Ramakrishna Mission near Kolkata, the Aurobindo Ashram in Pondicherry and the Golden Temple in Amritsar, thousands of miles apart. There are more such places around India where desi visitors are anything but the kind of Ugly Indian Tourist that locals complain about from Goa to Gangtok, Kashmir to Kanyakumari. That just begs the question why Indians are so badly behaved in many other places.An overwhelming majority of those who come to Kamarpukur and Joyrambati are devotees. They, therefore, know the sanctity of those places and behave accordingly. The same is true of the sacred precincts at Belur, Pondicherry and Amritsar. But why is the same courtesy not extended to all places they visit? Do only the divine merit courtesy, cleanliness and calm? The public's behaviour at these places show that Indians can be model visitors when we want to be.At Kamarpukur and Joyrambati it is hard to be anything but ideal visitors, though. There's something about the cumulative effect of their soothing tranquillity broken only by birdsong and trees rustling in the autumn breeze, the fresh flowers artfully arranged around the statues of Sri Ramkrishna and Maa Sarada Devi, and the smiling sanyasis telling stories of the divine couple's limitless humanity and humbleness... On the journey back to Kolkata, our hearts were full.

Jensen Huang controversy puts Southeast Asia’s AI chip trade under scrutiny
articles.summary: Chip and data-centre operators in Southeast Asia are bracing for tighter scrutiny after reports linking former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing put Singapore and Malaysia in the spotlight, industry executives and analysts told Reuters.The controversy has prompted US lawmakers from both parties to push for stronger restrictions on China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and intensified scrutiny of Nvidia’s role in US national security.Washington already restricts exports of Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips to China to protect US leadership in the sector. Lawmakers are now seeking to close a loophole that allows Chinese companies to rent computing power from overseas data centres and remotely access systems equipped with restricted chips.Any tougher regulations could include new export controls and licensing requirements for shipments to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore, the Wall Street Journal reported.Also Read | Anthropic IPO share orders from China are said to be rebuffedAlice Huang, the businesswoman suspected of spying for China, previously worked as an executive at Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed. The company has subsidiaries in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Australia and the US.Singapore authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since February last year over possible false declarations related to server purchases and other alleged offences.“After this case, every operator in the chain will be expected to know its end user. Southeast Asian operators will still get Nvidia chips, but proof of where every chip sits and who it serves is now part of the product,” Ke Yan, head of research at Singapore-based investment research firm Shenton Research, told Reuters.A ‘post-DeepSeek moment’Southeast Asia’s data-centre industry has grown rapidly as global technology companies expand their AI infrastructure.Malaysia has approved 385.7 billion ringgit ($94.67 billion) of data-centre-related investment since 2021, according to the country’s trade ministry. Thailand had 42 data centres representing 3,400 megawatts of IT capacity and about 750 billion baht ($22.58 billion) of investment as of February, while Indonesia’s market was valued at $2.81 billion in 2025.Gary Goh, CEO of Malaysia-based data-centre consultancy Sprint DC, described the prospect of tighter US rules as a “post-DeepSeek moment.”“Once the new rules are out, there will be a lot more restrictions for countries like Malaysia. There could be a short- to medium-term market shock to the Malaysian data centre market,” Goh said.For live updates on US Markets, click hereThe AI boom has supported economic growth across the region. Singapore raised its annual growth forecast in August to between 4.5% and 5.5%, from 2% to 4%, citing the AI cycle. In Malaysia, an increase in data-centre projects helped the construction sector grow 6% in the third quarter of 2026.The trade ministries of Singapore and Malaysia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Malaysia said Thursday that it was considering legislation that would allow the government to monitor data-centre operations, including the use of high-performance chips. Authorities said they needed to ensure that chips subject to US restrictions were imported for domestic use rather than re-exported.An investor and CEO of an Asian neocloud company, who asked not to be identified, said he spent Friday morning consulting lawyers in the US.“Everyone is still figuring out... Maybe every time you export something, there will be additional process to go through. We are worried about more scrutiny which will make it longer for chips to come through,” the CEO said.Singapore said in February 2025 that entities operating in the country accounted for 22% of Nvidia’s chip sales, although only 1% of the chips physically entered Singapore. Authorities have also charged a fifth person in a case involving alleged AI-server fraud.Region expected to withstand tighter rulesSome analysts said tighter controls were unlikely to derail the data-centre expansion in Singapore and Malaysia.“Singapore itself will be more stringent; I think it’s a natural thing to happen. Singapore will tighten rules, and the US will tighten rules, but I don’t think this will harm Singapore’s and Malaysia’s prospects of buying chips,”  Jarick Seet, head of small- and mid-cap equities at Maybank, told Reuters.A senior executive at a Singapore chipmaker, who declined to be identified, said Huang’s departure could make it more difficult for Chinese companies to obtain US chips while potentially improving availability elsewhere.“With Jensen out, the Chinese will have a harder time getting chips from the US. Maybe it is not a bad thing for the non-US people who will have more access to chips.”The executive said companies could also redirect investment to Southeast Asia if Democratic electoral victories in data-centre-heavy US states such as Texas and Georgia slow the development of new facilities.“Those companies are going to look elsewhere and likely come to countries that can offer them land and deals and power,” the executive said. “Even if we lose a chunk of the China business, I think we will get other companies coming looking for compute.”(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

articles.title: India says foreign goods can overstay
articles.summary: The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC)  introduced greater flexibility for foreign businesses and organisations on Friday, bringing goods into India temporarily by allowing senior customs officials to extend the existing four-month stay limit under the ATA Carnet system.The move will benefit foreign exhibitors, businesses, media organisations and other international participants who need to bring equipment, commercial samples or professional goods into India for a limited period. Until now, such goods were generally required to be re-exported within four months of their import.Under the revised provision, Principal Chief Commissioners of Customs and Chief Commissioners of Customs can approve an extension beyond the four months if they consider it necessary in the public interest.However, the extended period cannot go beyond the validity of the respective ATA Carnet."Provided also that where the Principal Chief Commissioner of Customs or the Chief Commissioner of Customs, as the case may be, is satisfied that it is necessary in the public interest so to do, may extend the aforesaid period of four months by such further period as it may deem fit, not exceeding the period of validity of the A.T.A. Carnet," said a memo from the Department of Revenue.What changes under the revised ATA Carnet rules?The amendment gives senior customs officials the authority to grant additional time for temporarily imported goods to remain in India.Previously, the four-month limit applied under the relevant customs notification, leaving limited room for businesses and organisations that needed more time before sending their goods back.With the latest change, the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner of Customs can assess individual cases and allow an extension where circumstances justify it.The additional time will depend on the official's assessment, but there is one important restriction: the extension must remain within the validity period of the ATA Carnet. This means the new provision does not allow goods to stay in India indefinitely.The amendment has been made to Notification No. 4/2018-Customs, dated January 18, 2018, by inserting an additional proviso under condition (vi).What is the ATA Carnet system and how does it work?An ATA Carnet is an international customs document that allows goods to enter a country temporarily without the importer having to pay customs duties at the time of import, subject to compliance with the applicable conditions.Often described as a passport for goods, the document simplifies customs procedures for businesses and individuals transporting professional equipment, commercial samples and exhibition materials across international borders.The system is particularly useful for companies participating in overseas trade fairs, exhibitions and business events. It also helps media organisations and professionals who need to carry specialised equipment across countries for temporary assignments.However, the duty-free facility comes with an important condition: the goods must be re-exported within the permitted period.

articles.title: Why Jensen Huang will lose  ₹900 crore after Nvidia exit — just 0.08% of his  ₹11.5 lakh crore fortune
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is set to forfeit  ₹900 crore ($108 million) in unvested Nvidia stock awards following his reported exit. The amount is just 0.08% of his estimated  ₹11.5 lakh crore fortune, with nearly 97% of his wealth tied to Nvidia shares.
